title: Runtime experimentation blueprint and hypothesis protocol
author: Maya Chen
body:
Overview

Purpose: This document defines a standardized, repeatable blueprint for formulating hypotheses, instrumenting experiments, and executing cross-layer runtime experiments that span runtime architecture, kernel scheduling, profiling playbooks, benchmarking suites, runbooks and release verification. It codifies guardrails for safety, data collection contracts, and an escalation path for regressions detected during experiments.

Audience: runtime engineers, SREs, performance researchers, release managers, and solutions engineers who run or consume inference experiments.

Scope and high-level principles

- Keep experiments scoped to a single independent variable wherever possible (e.g., scheduler policy, kernel variant, KV warmup window).
- Measure both application-visible metrics (p50/p95/p99 latency, error rate, token cost) and internal kernel signals (occupancy, kernel queue depth, preemption count, batch composition).
- Use shadow channels and low-risk canaries for disruptive changes; require automatic fallback for any change affecting P99 by >25% or cost by >15% in production-like traffic.
- Maintain reproducibility: every experiment must have an ID, input corpus, and synthetic traffic profile attached to the run artifact.

Roles and ownership

1. Experiment owner (single point): responsible for hypothesis, orchestration, runbook, and final report. (Typically the engineer proposing the change.)
2. Observability owner: ensures traces, metrics and sampled traces are available and annotated with experiment_id.
3. SRE reviewer: verifies safety windows, capacity headroom, and rollback plan for production canaries.
4. Release manager: gates experiment-to-release handoff and signs off acceptance criteria.

Hypothesis lifecycle (protocol)

1. Formulate hypothesis: 1–2 sentence statement (e.g., "Switching kernel-variant X to f32->int8 delta path reduces P50 by 18% for short sequences without increasing P99 by >5%.")
2. Define primary/secondary metrics: primary = P99 tail latency; secondary = token cost per million tokens, preemption rate, GPU stall time.
3. Create experiment specification: include traffic corpus, seed RNG, workload mix (inference/generation/chat/embedding), concurrency shape, and warmup steps. Use the experiment template.
4. Baseline capture: run at least three baseline runs across different cluster nodes (same family) and record statistical distribution.
5. Run treatment: execute change with identical traffic; collect same signals.
6. Statistical test: use non-parametric comparison (e.g., Mann–Whitney U) for latency distributions and bootstrap confidence for cost metrics.
7. Acceptance rules: pre-declared thresholds (see acceptance table). If a treatment fails, follow rollback runbook.

Experiment specification template (text)

- experiment_id: REX-2026-<short-id>
- hypothesis: short sentence
- target_cluster: hetero-gpu-pool-eu
- model_variant: gptx-2b-quantized-v2
- scheduler_profile: experimental-low-latency-priority
- traffic_profile: mixture {chat:40%, gen:40%, embedding:20%}, seed: 42
- synthetic_corpus: s3://redwood-experiments/corpora/voice-assistant-2025-v2
- duration: 30m warmup + 60m measurement
- observability_tags: [experiment_id, run_id, owner]

Telemetry contract (required signals)

Every experiment run must include the following time-aligned signals:

- request: request_id, timestamp, route, model_variant, sequence_length_in, sequence_length_out, token_count
- latency: service_pod_p99/95/50, kernel_dispatch_latency_ms, kernel_execution_ms, queue_wait_ms
- kernel: kernel_variant, batch_size_at_dispatch, preempted (bool), preemption_reason, occupancy_percent
- resource: gpu_util_percent, gpu_mem_free_mb, nvlink_errors, node_temperature_celsius
- cost: internal_token_cost_usd_per_1m, kernel_cuda_time_ms
- traces: sampled_trace (include kernel span IDs)

Scheduling & kernel test harness

- Use the harness utility at tools/runtime-experiments/harness to define: workload mix, artificial jitter, and backpressure injection. Example CLI:

  ./harness run --experiment REX-2026-001 --profile mixed-chat-gen --duration 5400 --seed 42 --trace-sample-rate 0.02

- Kernel-scheduler knobs to exercise: priority-weight (0–100), batch-slice-ms, preemption-window-ms, admission-rate-per-sec. Record each knob change in the run metadata.

- Synthetic failure injection: in non-prod clusters, run controlled preemption bursts to observe contention behavior: inject_preempt --rate 5/s --duration 60s --target kernel-variant=kv-prefetch

Benchmarking acceptance criteria (table as text)

| Metric | Baseline target | Treatment pass requirement | Notes |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| P50 latency (ms) | 12–20 | No increase >10% (prefer decrease) | Short-sequence workload |
| P95 latency (ms) | 32–60 | No increase >15% | Multi-tenant noise tolerant |
| P99 latency (ms) | 110–220 | No increase >5% (hard gate) | If >5%, require canary-only rollout & SRE approval |
| Error rate (5xx) | <0.05% | No increase >2x baseline | Hard gate |
| Token cost per 1M | $1.20 | No increase >10% | Estimate from kernel_cuda_time |
| Preemption rate | 0–2% | No increase >3x | Investigate starvation |

(Note: treat the P99 gate as blocking for production rollouts.)

Profiling playbook integration

- When an experiment exercises kernel changes, attach a profiling run using the standard profiler: profiler run --experiment <id> --collect kernel-metrics,trace-heap,occupancy --duration 10m
- Capture at least 1s-resolution kernel spans and a sampled set of full-request traces (1 trace per 5k requests).
- Use the profiler output to create a causal latency map and annotate preemption/splice points.

Runbook: regression triage (high-level steps)

1. Detect: alert triggers when P99 > baseline * 1.05 or error-rate spikes. Tag alert with experiment_id.
2. Contain: immediately stop the experiment traffic or throttle to 10% of original. If production canary, initiate immediate rollback.
3. Collect: gather last 15 minutes of metrics, 100 sampled traces, kernel occupancy histograms and recent scheduler decisions.
4. Hypothesis stack: compare dispatch batch sizes, kernel_variant usage, and preemption_events between baseline and treatment.
5. Mitigate: apply mitigation recipes in order: a) revert scheduler profile to stable, b) enable admission-limiter, c) pin to previous kernel_variant.
6. Postmortem: owner writes incident note within 48 hours with root cause and remediation plan.

Release notes checklist (for changes touching runtime stack)

- Include experiment IDs used for benchmarking.
- Summarize acceptance metrics and whether any additional SRE mitigations were required.
- Highlight known limitations and observed anomalies.
- Attach reproducible run artifacts: traffic profile, synthetic corpus, raw profiler output.

Known issues and workarounds (examples)

- ID KI-2026-42: Intermittent kernel handoff timeout when batch_slice_ms <= 3. Symptoms: elevated P95 and occasional request timeout (upstream grpc deadline). Workaround: set batch_slice_ms >= 5 or enable cooperative-preempt fallback.
- ID KI-2026-57: KVCache warmup misalignment on heterogeneous pools. Symptoms: cold-start P50 spikes for embedding-heavy routes. Workaround: pre-warm KV cache using warmup traffic job; use kv_warmup_hint in deployment config.
- ID KI-2026-88: Trace sampling amplification under high concurrency causing trace-collector backpressure. Symptoms: missing kernel spans in profiler output. Workaround: reduce trace-sample-rate to 0.005 during high concurrency and rely on shadow channels for full fidelity.

Safeguards for production experiments

- Any experiment running on production-labeled pools must:
  - have an SRE reviewer with signed approval,
  - be limited to max 5% of production traffic during initial canary,
  - include an automated fallback plan that triggers on P99 violation or error-rate > 2x baseline.

Artifact retention and reproducibility

- Store experiment run artifacts under s3://redwood-experiments/runs/<experiment_id> including: run_metadata.json, profiler.tgz, metrics.csv, sampled_traces.tgz, baseline_snapshot.json.
- Attach a short reproducibility note summarizing exact cluster topology, seed, and version pins for the runtime, scheduler, and kernels.

Quick examples

- Example kernel config snippet (YAML):

  scheduler:
    name: experimental-low-latency-priority
    priority_weight: 80
    batch_slice_ms: 6
    preemption_window_ms: 12
    admission_rate_per_sec: 1200

- Example rollout CLI to start a canary (production-safe):

  ./orchestrator rollout --cluster prod-eu --deployment my-model:v2026-07 --canary-percent 3 --monitor-metrics p99,errors --fallback revert --experiment-id REX-2026-101

Post-experiment reporting structure

- Executive summary (1 paragraph)
- Baseline vs treatment metric tables and distribution plots (P50/P95/P99)
- Key profiler findings and kernel-level causal map
- Acceptance decision (Pass/Fail/Conditional) and recommended rollout path
- Artifacts: links to s3 run folder, dashboards, and traces

Appendix: experiment scoring rubric (how to pick winners)

- Score components (weights): latency improvement (40%), cost improvement (30%), stability (20%), operational complexity (10%).
- Score interpretation: >70 = recommended rollout; 50–70 = gated rollout with more shadow testing; <50 = discard and iterate.

Contact and escalation
